title: Test Your Understanding: Design a Rate Limiter
description: Algorithms, Redis, distributed limits, and HTTP semantics — trade-offs from the case study.

questions.question: Why is a fixed-window counter (e.g. 1000 req/min) problematic at window boundaries?

options.text: It uses too much Redis memory
Clients can send 2× the limit in a short span straddling the reset
It cannot work with API keys

questions.explanation: 999 requests at 0:59 and 999 at 1:00 yields ~1998 in two seconds despite a 1000/min rule. Sliding window or token bucket avoids the cliff.

questions.question: Token bucket is often preferred for public APIs because:

options.text: It allows bounded bursts while enforcing a sustained refill rate
It is identical to leaky bucket

questions.explanation: Capacity B allows burst up to B tokens; refill rate r caps steady-state throughput. Matches real client traffic better than strict constant leak.

questions.question: Per-server in-memory rate limits fail in a cluster because:

options.text: Each server enforces the full quota — effective limit ≈ N × limit
Token bucket cannot run in process

questions.explanation: Clients round-robin across N nodes and get N times the intended budget unless counters are shared (Redis) or enforced at a central gateway.

questions.question: Redis Lua scripts for token bucket primarily solve:

options.text: Atomic read-modify-write races on concurrent requests

questions.explanation: Without atomicity, two concurrent requests both read the same token count and both pass — over-admission. Lua runs atomically on the Redis server.

questions.question: Enforcing rate limits at the API gateway (before app services) helps because:

options.text: Abusive traffic is rejected before consuming DB pools and business logic

questions.explanation: Limiter after auth yields a stable key (API key/user). Denying early protects downstream resources that are expensive to scale.

questions.question: On rate limit denial, returning Retry-After primarily helps:

options.text: Clients back off instead of retry-storming the API
Bypass the limit for VIP users

questions.explanation: Retry-After (and X-RateLimit-* headers) signal cooperative backoff — reduces retry storms that worsen outages.

questions.question: Fail-open (allow traffic when Redis is unavailable) always protects backend capacity during an attack.
questions.explanation: Fail-open preserves availability but removes protection exactly when limiter store fails — often during overload. Many APIs fail closed for external traffic or use local emergency buckets.

questions.question: Good rate limit keys for authenticated APIs include: (Select all that apply)

options.text: ip:{address} as fallback for anonymous traffic
Always only ip — never user identity

questions.explanation: Authenticated identity gives fair per-tenant limits. IP-only breaks behind NAT; IP fallback helps anonymous endpoints.
